items.title: vLLM now matches DeepSeek's DeepInfer engine on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode, using half the expert parallelism
items.summary: The vLLM team says its decode throughput curves for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash now line up with DeepInfer, the engine DeepSeek open-sourced, on DeepSeek's own decode setup for batch sizes 8 to 256. vLLM gets there at DEP32 while DeepInfer uses EP64DP64. The gain came from pulling in DeepSeek's open kernels and tuning prefill and decode. Earlier this week the gap was about 6 percent.

reasons: Numbers come only from a vLLM chart image; no benchmark script or blog linked yet.

items.title: LlamaIndex releases OCRia-1, a 4B document parsing model that leads ParseBench by 12 points
items.summary: OCRia-1 is a 4 billion parameter vision-language model that now powers LlamaParse. LlamaIndex reports 87.4 overall on ParseBench, 12.1 points ahead of the next parser, and top table scores on olmOCR-bench (92.9), PulseBench-Tab (84.1) and fr-bench-pdf2md. It turns charts into HTML tables of data points (85.1 on ParseBench charts) and keeps superscripts, checkboxes and LaTeX math. Training used about 100k hard pages with supervised fine-tuning plus RL with verifiable rewards.

reasons: The blog does not say whether weights are released or only available through LlamaParse.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max) enters Agent Arena at #11, the top open model, at a $1.03 median cost per task
items.summary: Arena reports Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max) at +7.6 percent net improvement across more than 4,000 real agentic sessions, up from #25 for Kimi K3 (Max). That would make it the highest-ranked open model, ahead of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, once the promised open weights ship. By category it ranks #8 in Work, #9 in Code and #10 in Chat. Its median cost per task is 13 percent lower than the previous variant.

reasons: Replies point out it is #8 on user sentiment but only #26 on confirmed task success, so the headline rank leans on sentiment.
Net improvement is measured against the average model, not against Kimi K3, and that baseline moves over time.

items.reception: Mixed. Replies praise the price, while several note the gap between the sentiment rank and the confirmed success rank.

items.title: Nous Research's advanced-delegation plugin lets Hermes Agent route each subagent to a different model
items.summary: A user set up two routes on Nous Portal with the new plugin and gave one prompt containing two jobs. The main agent sent a short summary task to Claude Haiku 5.5, back in 3.0 seconds, and a logic puzzle to Claude Opus 5.5 at high reasoning, solved in 9.3 seconds, choosing each route on its own. The full run is shown in a video.

items.title: Study: frontier models rewriting their own agent harness gain only 2.8 points on held-out ARC-AGI-3 games
items.summary: Each model writes a full harness from a fixed coding bootstrap, plays five development games, then rewrites the whole codebase twice, with scoring on 20 games that never feed the rewrites. Across 27 lineages, two rewrites raise held-out scores by 2.80 points and the 95 percent interval crosses zero. Gains on the development games overstate held-out gains, cost-cutting revisions often lower scores, and human-steered harnesses still score higher.

items.title: Paper: coding agents pick skill granularity at runtime, falling back from macro skills to primitive tool calls
items.summary: For each task the agent chooses primitive tool calls, a macro skill, or a macro skill that drops to primitive steps when it fails. A controller decides from task structure, execution state and earlier macro failures, and a finite-state executor handles the fallback as an explicit transition rather than an ad hoc retry. In a 12-task routing study a learned router reaches 100 percent success where a hand-written heuristic fails.

reasons: The routing study covers only 12 tasks.
